questions.stem: Olive oil is liquid at room temperature while butter is solid. Both are lipids. What structural difference explains this?

options.text: Olive oil contains shorter hydrocarbon chains than butter
Olive oil contains more unsaturated (C=C double bond) fatty acid chains, which have kinks that prevent close packing
Butter contains more water than olive oil
Olive oil is a pure substance while butter is a mixture

questions.explanation: Unsaturated fatty acids have C=C double bonds that create kinks in the hydrocarbon chain. These kinks prevent molecules from packing closely together, resulting in weaker intermolecular forces and lower melting points (liquid oils). Saturated fats like butter have straight chains that pack tightly, giving stronger forces and higher melting points (solid fats).

questions.stem: Soap is made by heating fats or oils with sodium hydroxide solution. This process is called saponification. What are the products?

options.text: Glycerol and fatty acids
Soap (sodium salts of fatty acids) and glycerol
Esters and water
Ethanol and sodium chloride

questions.explanation: Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of fats/oils (which are esters of glycerol and fatty acids). Sodium hydroxide breaks the ester bonds, producing glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids (soap). For example: fat + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3 soap molecules. The sodium salts of the fatty acids are what we know as soap.

questions.stem: A soap molecule has a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) tail. How does this structure help soap clean greasy stains?

options.text: The soap chemically breaks down the grease into carbon dioxide and water
The hydrophobic tails embed in the grease while the hydrophilic heads remain in the water, breaking the grease into tiny droplets that wash away
The soap dissolves the grease into a single phase
The soap heats up the water, melting the grease

questions.explanation: Soap molecules form structures called micelles around grease droplets. The hydrophobic tails point inward and dissolve into the grease, while the hydrophilic heads point outward into the water. This surrounds the grease in tiny droplets (emulsification) that can be washed away. The grease is not chemically changed — it is physically broken up and suspended in water.

questions.stem: Vegetable oils can be hardened by reacting them with hydrogen gas using a nickel catalyst. A food manufacturer partially hydrogenates sunflower oil. What is the result?

options.text: The oil becomes completely liquid
Some C=C double bonds are converted to C-C single bonds, making the oil semi-solid and suitable for making margarine
The oil breaks down into glycerol and fatty acids
The oil becomes a gas

questions.explanation: Partial hydrogenation converts some (but not all) C=C double bonds in the unsaturated fatty acids to C-C single bonds. This partially straightens the chains, allowing slightly more packing and raising the melting point. The oil becomes semi-solid — ideal for spreads like margarine. Full hydrogenation would make it completely solid.

questions.stem: Detergents have largely replaced soap for laundry because soap does not work well in hard water. What happens when soap is used in hard water?

options.text: The soap dissolves too quickly to be effective
The soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water to form an insoluble scum, wasting soap
The soap makes the water too alkaline for fabrics
Hard water makes soap more effective than in soft water

questions.explanation: Hard water contains dissolved calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) ions. Soap anions react with these ions to form insoluble calcium or magnesium salts of fatty acids — the grey scum seen in hard water areas. This wastes soap and leaves deposits on clothes. Synthetic detergents do not form scum with hard water ions, making them more effective.
